en: This very horse Tootoru
Had appeared by providence
From the desert of Mediyan,
From the pass of It-Kyyan,
Where no cawing crow was found,
No croaking raven flew,
There was no grass for beasts to chew,
No water for man to swallow—
From the desert no dog could cross,
From the shore where no living thing roamed.
He was encountered as a two-year-old
And found as a three-year-old.
He was raised in a dark place,
With an amulet fastened to his head;
The blood-drinking brass-beaked crone
Tested him there and approved him.
No other soul could ride him,
And he could not refrain from speaking.
“Hold and turn my horse’s mouth;
What will Tootoru say now?
Wait, woman Chürök, stand still!
No human speaks such words—
What is my beast, my bay, saying?”
Thus spoke brave Kyyaz,
Now raging, now calming,
A sheathless sword strapped to him;
Blood-stained Kyyaz raged.
When the key struck his forehead,
Tootoru, being a swift steed,
Staggered in circles,
Swaying like one dazed,
Yet did not topple and fall;
He shied away, then recovered.
The bay horse that had been speaking
Lost the use of his tongue.
His forelock fell over his eyes;
The hair tassel split his forehead
A full span wide.
Subdued by the blow,
The poor bay horse
Had his speaking tongue bound.
Alas, that woman Aichürök
Raised her stately head like a banner,
Turned a woman’s head into a warrior’s,
And struck the speaking steed
Down level with the black earth;
She deafened his hearing ears
And bound his tongue.
Brave Kyyaz of the Jediger
Was that day in Jeti-Özön,
In the pleasure garden of the fortress,
Seated there
Upon his throne, ruling the people.
Such was Kyyaz when you saw him,
His bluish fist as large as a knob;
Such was his appearance.
He raged like a blue-maned lion,
As insight came to him from the unseen;
He roared in anger,
Calling out to Aichürök,
His bellow splitting heads,
His shout splitting stones:
“Accursed Chürök, wait there!
If he speaks, that is my learning;
Tootoru is my wing.
When grave trouble befalls an honored man,
When a black day weighs upon his soul,
Though you came to us as a captive slave,
You have shown your valor.
Like a ravine untouched by wind,
You have proved yourself a mountain pass.
You have shown yourself a lion
Who could subdue the peoples of the world.
If you are a hero, if you are a lion,
Your terror is like a club-sized fist.
You charged and shouted,
Calling out, ‘Aichürök!’
If you are mighty, if you are a lion,
If you truly are hero Kyyaz,
Would you behave like this?
Why do you shout so?
Shall I go deliberately to the village,
Saying, ‘My lord, has the world ever seen the like?’
If you would slaughter me, here is my head;
If a woman has committed a crime,
First make your horse speak.”
So Aichürök spoke,
Seized the reins of the plunging Tootoru,
And turned his head;
With these words your Chürök
Stood speaking to Kyyaz.
For all the ages until now,
Peerless Kyyaz, you have done wrong;
Time and again,
You have scorned us as slave women.
The sable cap upon your head—
Who has not worn one tilted proudly?
While fortune crowns his head,
Who has not gone about roaring?
At the sight of a champion,
How many enemies have not panicked?
I was that same Chürök,
But captivity brought my head to shame;
Among us, holy Kyyaz held supreme power.
Hero, we are slaves in your hands,
The bare ground where horses are tethered,
Wretches fallen into captivity.
Seized by bloodthirsty fury,
Unable to make the black earth crack
Beneath the weight of Kyyaz’s wrath,
He flailed about in anger,
Saying, “What did the horse say?”
Brave Kyyaz of the Jediger
Came running in a swagger.
Aichürök, Akun’s daughter,
Spoke these words:
“If your horse speaks, heed his tongue,
By your father’s grave, brave Kyyaz!
You refuse to grant the horse’s strength
To your lawfully wedded wife—
What a fool you are, Kyyaz!
Forty carpets from the winding pass—
I know the nature of this horse.
Let us pass before him
And hear him speak, since you claim
To be a holy man.
Make your horse speak, brave Kyyaz;
Though we are women, let us hear.
Can one who merely tends livestock and keeps a household
Be a hero such as you?
Is it right to call a wretch like you
A hero?
Hero, you have braced your black Zulfiqar sword
Against your side
As though an enemy had come to grapple with you.
From the wife you took under ancestral blessing,
You withheld your horse’s strength.
If you were ever a khan, it was in vain;
If you roar in anger,
You may cut off this poor head.
Among all your people filling Jeti-Özön,
Among the countless assembled throng,
My lord and hero, among your people
Was there no slave woman but me
For your mockery and amusement?
You hung that blood-spilling, keen-edged blade
From your wrist.
I see I was destined to suffer,
For rushing in heedlessly,
I see I was destined for disaster.
Cruel Aichürök, fair as the moon,
You are my treasure and my strength,
A bride lovely as the moon.
Delay brings grievous trouble—
I entrust Tootoru to you.
I gave you your choice from the herds;
Take my swift steed Tootoru.
I have been somewhat shamed, Aichürök;
Pour out my blood and take it in your leather flask!
Go to the herdsman and return;
Bring me quickly that poor fellow
Whom I found only when death was near.
Let my eyes behold him;
Bring him quickly back to me.”
Thus brave Kyyaz spoke,
Beginning a quarrel and hiding his intent,
Stirring up still greater trouble and strife:
“You were a lake, Chürök—overlook my fault!
Go safely and return unharmed;
Come back quickly and do not make me yearn.”
Thus he spoke to Chürök,
Striding away with wicked thoughts;
To the hapless woman fair as the moon
He entrusted the horse Tootoru.
Brave Kyyaz turned back,
Kyyaz the warrior with the fierce mustache;
When you looked at his mustache,
It resembled a sack from Bukhara.
Each of his shoulders was immense,
As though two men sat upon them;
When you looked at his two cheeks,
They were like two sated Dungans.
Such was his aspect when you saw him,
Like a bloodthirsty khan,
Like a mighty ruler of nations.
Kyyaz turned and remained behind,
Entrusting his bay horse:
If you will not ride him, here is the road;
If you would push him, here is the ravine;
If you would bind him, here are his legs.
Many are the cares within my heart;
God stands above your greatness.
Kyyaz, your anger has brought no good;
Time and again,
You have not curbed your violence.
Because my beast spoke,
You fly into a rage.
Let us pass before him,
Ask your beast to speak,
And, hero, though we are women,
Let us hear.”
She turned Tootoru’s mouth,
And before brave Kyyaz
Your dear sister-in-law Aichürök
Stood pulling the bay horse’s reins.
Wearing a robe patterned with blue flowers,
Brave Kyyaz, had you seen him,
Raged like a blue-maned lion;
He ran forward, heaving and panting,
His knees bending toward the ground,
His weapons set in order,
A naked sword strapped to him.
He pulled the reins
And turned the tireless steed Tootoru’s head.
Such was brave Kyyaz when you saw him;
As the bay horse swayed and plunged,
He stood stroking its forelock.
The great bay horse neighed,
But its forelock did not part,
And it showed no sign of speaking.
He turned it this way and stroked it,
But the great bay horse said nothing.
The bay horse had no words to speak,
And brave Kyyaz, enraged,
Was disgraced before Chürök,
The woman lovely as the moon.
“You said Tootoru had spoken—
I will smash you down upon the earth!
Across the rough and broken steppe,
Along ridges no horse can tread,
I will stretch my stride like an argali.
I will deliver punishment
To that deceitful, cunning woman!
If a ravine with cliff-bound hollows appears,
If a deadly mountain rises,
I will wheel and twist my neck.
That beautiful woman,
That cunning and clever infidel,
That woman with her tinkling laugh,
That infidel who thinks herself so bold—
If I do not veer and wrench my neck,
If I do not bring her crashing
Against the deep black earth below!
I will break her arms and leave them dangling;
That mincing wretch—
I will end her life in this fashion
And cast her sprawling on her back,
Unless I avenge the blow she struck me.
Though my flesh be torn apart like a sheep’s,
Though my path be straightened like a felt mat,
I will open my mouth like a cavern
And scatter blood-flecked white foam
Across my chest.
I will traverse the four corners
Of the whole round world forty times.
My back shall bend without arching,
